transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-03 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~47m | Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Lena (CTO Veridian), Raj (ML Eng), Sophie (PM), Ben (SRE)

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, um, thanks for joining. quick agenda — tokens per dollar recap, caching audit, batching tradeoffs, and next steps. Maya, you want to kick off with the numbers?

[00:18] Maya: Yeah sure, I pulled the pilot runs from last week, so these are rough numbers — we measured tokens/sec/$ using the baseline model variant (rwd-4x) with current quant and default batch strategy. overall median was ~1,200 tokens/sec per dollar at 512 context, but when we bumped to 2k context it fell to ~680.

[00:40] Raj: wait, 1,200 tokens per dollar, um that's median or mean?

[00:44] Maya: median, we also have mean which is a bit skewed by a couple of large outputs. p95 latency at 512 was around 210ms on hosted, p95 went up to 650ms at 2k context.

[01:02] Sophie: that's helpful — can you map that to our user flows? most of our async generation is in the 1k to 2k space.

[01:10] Maya: yeah so for the summarization flow (avg output 350 tokens, prompt 900 tokens) you land closer to the 680 tokens/sec/$ number. we also tested prefix caching for the first 800 tokens and saw substantial savings.

[01:25] Lena: how substantial? give us % because that's what execs will ask for.

[01:29] Maya: with prefix caching enabled and a 45% hit rate on the sampled traffic, tokens billed dropped roughly 32% and effective tokens/sec/$ improved to about 1,000. if you can push hit rates to 60% for repeat queries, that goes to ~1,260 tokens/sec/$ — caveat, these are synthetic aggregate numbers.

[01:52] Raj: that 45% hit rate was on our dev traffic sample, right? not prod-shaped?

[01:58] Maya: correct — sample from the pilot's staging feed. Ben: did you see anything surprising in SRE logs?

[02:05] Ben: logs look ok, small amount of 503s during the 2k stress windows, those aligned with autoscaler cooldowns. nothing persistent. we did capture KV lookup latencies — average 4ms but with a tail to 90ms on cold shards.

[02:24] Jared: cold shards — that's the thing we'd try to smooth with caching warmers or pre-warms right?

[02:29] Maya: yeah, pre-warm and smarter shard routing. also consider backend-local prefix cache (for dedicated) vs global hosted cache — tradeoffs in cost and consistency.

[02:40] Lena: can you explain the dedicated vs hosted cache economics quickly? we need the quick elevator version.

[02:45] Maya: sure. hosted — you get a shared global cache, low ops, but you pay per-token and have less predictability. dedicated — you pay reserved capacity (GPU pool) and can co-locate prefix cache on the same nodes, which reduces KV lookup cross-network cost and reduces cold-start tails; that improves tokens/sec/$ for heavy, repeat workloads but requires a commit.

[03:08] Sophie: what's the breakeven point? like qps or monthly tokens where dedicated makes sense?

[03:13] Maya: ballpark, for your workload shape with 60% cache hits and median response sizes, we estimate breakeven at ~4.5B tokens/month. i'll put the exact scenarios in the benchmark sheet.

[03:26] Raj: okay good. on batching, earlier you mentioned batch=64 — we saw better throughput but tail latency ballooned. can you walk the tradeoff again?

[03:35] Maya: absolutely. batching increases tokens/sec by improving GPU utilization. at batch=64 we saw throughput increase 2.7x versus batch=8, but p95 latency increased by about 3x in the hosted runs, because batching groups requests and some waiting accumulates at the leader. continuous batching strategies (smarter cutoffs) can reduce tail but add complexity.

[03:58] Raj: is continuous batching supported in the current runtime?

[04:01] Maya: yes, it's in the runtime — but the tuning knobs are sensitive: max-delay, max-batch-size, prioritization for low-latency routes. we can configure per-route SLOs so user-facing short flows get lower max-delay.

[04:17] Lena: any quick wins to get better tokens/sec/$ without committing to Dedicated?

[04:21] Maya: three things: 1) prefix caching on top-20 prompts (easy, big wins), 2) modest batch tuning (move from 8 to 16/32 for non-interactive routes), 3) quantization profile change — we tested q4f16 for the rwd-4x and saw about 12% cost improvement with imperceptible quality delta for your eval set.

[04:44] Sophie: the q4f16 results — we want that in writing and sample outputs, please.

[04:48] Jared: will do, i'll attach the eval diffs. Maya, can you walk us through the caching audit you ran?

[04:55] Maya: sure — small table summary: sampled 48k requests over 72h, top-20 prefixes accounted for 38% of requests. LRU cache with 10k entries gave 45% hit. TTL was set to 24h in the staging run. We also saw that some prefixes are high-entropy (unique ids), those don't benefit and should be whitelisted to bypass cache.

[05:19] Raj: which prefixes are high-entropy? any that we can normalize?

[05:23] Maya: the user-id and session tokens, also timestamps embedded in prompts. if you normalize those placeholders or move them to structured context rather than raw prompt, hit rates jump.

[05:34] Ben: we can do normalization on our side, but we'll need a clear mapping of which tokens to scrub.

[05:38] Maya: we'll annotate the top-20 list with suggested normalization patterns.

[05:42] Lena: about tokens/sec/$ metric — are we using the same costing assumptions as last week? I thought there was a discount applied for 2nd tier usage.

[05:50] Jared: good call, right now the numbers Maya quoted assume hosted list pricing. if you apply your committed usage tier and include prefix cache savings you'd see about 18% better unit econ than the quoted hosted baseline; we'll send scenarios for committed reserved capacity tomorrow.

[06:05] Sophie: we also want a run that mimics mixed traffic: 60% async batch, 40% interactive. can we parameterize that?

[06:12] Maya: yes, that's a separate load profile. Raj, can you define the exact ratio and expected QPS, and we'll template the load generator.

[06:19] Raj: sure — I'll do that after the call.

[06:22] Jared: quick note on fallbacks — we configured a lower-cost model (rwd-4s) as a graceful degrade. Memory/quality tradeoff is small for short summaries but bigger for long-form completions. worth testing for tail events.

[06:34] Lena: what's the rollback behavior if fallback triggers too often? we don't want inconsistent outputs.

[06:39] Maya: we can set a strict policy: only fallback when latency or error rate breaches thresholds and log all fallback events to a dedicated stream so you can audit. Also, A/B rollout allows comparing outputs for parity before enabling fallback broadly.

[06:54] Sophie: anything on security? our legal team wants KMS integration and audit logs for all model requests.

[07:00] Jared: Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations and fine-grained audit logs. for Private we can do customer-managed KMS and retain logs in your VPC. we'll schedule the security deep-dive with our security engineer.

[07:12] Lena: good. add SAML SSO and RBAC conversation to that deep-dive.

[07:17] Jared: noted.

[07:20] Maya: back to the data — i want to flag one oddity: in the 2k stress run we saw an unusual pattern where tokens/sec/$ briefly spiked because a batch merged many short queries; but p95 worsened. it's a statistical artifact but important when comparing median vs tail.

[07:38] Raj: yeah that's the batch-merging effect, we saw similar in our internal tests. can we add a per-route latency budget so critical flows don't get merged too long?

[07:46] Maya: yes, route-level max-delay and priority queuing. we'll propose defaults but you can tune.

[07:52] Ben: operational ask — can Redwood export the cache heatmap and per-shard cold-start trace? that'll help us repro cold shard behavior on our infra.

[07:59] Maya: yes, i can add an export to the shared sheet — it'll include timestamps, shard id, lookup latencies.

[08:07] Sophie: timeline recap?

[08:09] Jared: action items: Maya shares detailed benchmark sheet by Aug 6; Raj runs 48h throughput by Aug 10; schedule security deep-dive for week of Aug 17. we'll reconvene next Tuesday same time for results playback.

[08:25] Lena: sounds good, thanks everyone.

[08:28] Raj: quick clarifying Q — for the 48h run, do you want us to enable prefix caching or run cold?

[08:33] Maya: do both: first 24h cold, second 24h with cache warm (run a warm-up script). that'll show delta and realistic steady-state hit rate.

[08:43] Jared: perfect. i'll circulate notes and the benchmark link. thanks all.

[08:47] End of recording

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-hearings; speakers sometimes overlap; references to internal Redwood product names may be imperfect (e.g., rwd-4x, rwd-4s).
